target.thesis: For artificial speakers, acts whose content conditions include future conduct by the speaker (promising and similar commissives) depend on whether a unit capable of lasting through the satisfaction horizon is available, and scaffolding can supply one. Assertion has no such requirement, so artificial systems can come apart on the two acts.
target.headline: Whether an artificial system can perform a given speech act depends on whether that act type's felicity conditions require a speaker that persists until the act is satisfied. Assertion and advice need no persisting speaker, but promising and apologising do, so the current positions (quasi, proxy, proto, denial) cannot each be correct across act types.
target.target: Freiman and Miller's assertion-only quasi-testimony, and the tacit generalisation from assertion to speech acts in Williams and Bayne, Skiba and Green and Michel.
target.sketch: Freiman and Miller test artificial speakers almost wholly on assertion or testimony, and the later literature generalises from assertion to 'speech acts' (Skiba) or to apology in particular (Magnus et al.). Assertion is a synchronic act: its success conditions are met by the utterance and the hearer's uptake. Commissives and apologies are diachronic, because the speaker's future conduct is what satisfies or falsifies them. An LLM deployment offers several candidate speaker-units: the weights, the context-window instance, the persona, and the product or company. Each persists differently. The weights persist but are not 'in' the conversation. The instance ends with the window. The persona is individuated by prompt. The product persists but is a corporate agent. The key premise is that the speaker-unit must be individuated by the act type's satisfaction conditions, not fixed once for the whole system. On this premise, quasi-testimony or proto-assertion may be right for assertion while the proxy view is forced for promising and apology. A 'quasi-promise' would be incoherent, since a promise cannot be partly binding on no one. The positions are therefore indexed to act types, and the existing disputes come from treating assertion as the model case.

findings.part: Core diagnostic: for conversational agents, commissives and assertions come apart, and the difference turns on memory and persistence across time
findings.source: Authors not shown in the snippet, "In conversation with Artificial Intelligence: aligning language models with human values", arXiv 2209.00731, c. 2022
findings.what_they_say: <cite index="13-1,13-3">A commissive's validity depends on whether the commitment is honoured. This raises questions for conversational agents that lack memory or have only an episodic grasp of what they said earlier.</cite> <cite index="13-6,13-7">They add that conversational agents are well-placed to make some kinds of utterance but not all, and that this asymmetry may constrain what they are allowed to say.</cite>
findings.note: This already ties commissive failure to the lack of a persisting agent and says agents are better placed for some act types than others. I saw only a snippet. It does not individuate speaker-units, discuss scaffolding, or engage the quasi-testimony and proxy debates.

findings.part: The candidate speaker-units (weights, instance, persona, scaffolded system) and the claim that each persists differently
findings.source: "The Artificial Self: Characterising the landscape of AI identity" (arXiv 2603.11353), with the LessWrong discussion "Persona Self-replication experiment"; Beckmann & Butlin, "Where is the Mind? Persona Vectors and LLM Individuation", arXiv 2604.17031, 2026
findings.what_they_say: <cite index="52-1">The Artificial Self distinguishes identity scopes: the instance, the weights, the persona, the lineage, or the scaffolded system.</cite> <cite index="53-4,53-9">Beckmann & Butlin discuss the model and the virtual instance (the model as it runs in a single conversation).</cite> <cite index="55-2">They also discuss a persona view, on which the entity is defined by a system prompt or fine-tuning configuration.</cite>
findings.note: The unit inventory and the idea that a scaffolded system is a separate candidate are already in print. These sources do not index the choice of unit to speech-act type or to a satisfaction horizon.

findings.part: Product or company as the persisting unit, and the proxy view as the route to binding commitments
findings.source: Green & Michel, "Artificial intelligence and illocutionary force", 2022, as reported in Williams & Bayne, "Chatting with Bots", arXiv 2410.16645, and in the Springer survey "Against speech liberalism for generative AI", 2026
findings.what_they_say: <cite index="62-7,62-8">Williams & Bayne report that Green & Michel's main case is an AI deployed by a police department, whose outputs, such as traffic fines, are implicitly endorsed by the department.</cite> <cite index="58-6">A survey reads Green & Michel as holding that an artificial system may itself perform a speech act while acting for a person or institution whose commitments supply the normative basis.</cite>
findings.note: The corporate or institutional principal as the bearer of normative force is already the core of the proxy view. These are secondary descriptions, not Green & Michel's own text, and they treat it as an account of assertion and illocution generally, not of diachronic commissives.

findings.part: Named target: Freiman & Miller are assertion/testimony-only
findings.source: Freiman & Miller, "Can Artificial Entities Assert?", Oxford Handbook of Assertion, 2020
findings.what_they_say: <cite index="2-9">Quasi-testimony says technological devices can assert or testify under some conditions, without denying that humans and machines differ.</cite> The abstract lists four differences between humans and machines; none concerns speech acts other than assertion or testimony.
findings.note: The ascription holds at abstract level: the scope is assertion and testimony. I did not read the full text for remarks on other acts.

findings.part: Named target: Williams & Bayne's 'tacit generalisation' from assertion to speech acts
findings.source: Williams & Bayne, "Chatting with Bots: AI, Speech Acts, and the Edge of Assertion", Inquiry, 2024/2026
findings.what_they_say: <cite index="42-3,42-4">The paper asks whether chatbots can assert, through the Thesis of Chatbot Assertion.</cite> <cite index="42-8,42-9">It rejects proxy-assertion and fictionalism and argues for a category of proto-assertion.</cite>
findings.note: The thesis, arguments and proposed category are all about assertion. The 'speech acts' in the title is not shown to be a generalisation. I did not confirm from the full text whether they say anything about commissives.

findings.part: Named target: Skiba generalises from assertion to speech acts in general
findings.what_they_say: <cite index="31-1,31-2">Skiba asks whether LLMs can perform speech acts and shows how a norm-based argument against LLM assertion can be generalised to support a negative answer.</cite>
findings.note: The target holds the generalising view as ascribed. His route is uniform norm-based skepticism, not a difference between synchronic and diachronic acts, so the thesis's act-type split would be a rival to his generalisation, not an anticipation. I did not see how he treats promising specifically.

findings.part: Named target: Magnus et al. and the act-type-indexed result (a defence that works for assertion does not carry over to apology)
findings.source: Magnus, Buccella & D'Cruz, "Chatbot apologies: Beyond bullshit", AI and Ethics, 2025
findings.what_they_say: <cite index="22-10">Apology is a speech act which requires an agent with certain capacities, and chatbots lack them.</cite> <cite index="22-14">They also say the defence Mallory gives, of pretending that chatbots can assert, does not work for chatbots incapable of apologizing.</cite>
findings.note: This already indexes the verdict to act type, with a fictionalist or pretence defence for assertion and none for apology. Their ground is agent capacities and moral agency, not whether a speaker-unit lasts through a satisfaction horizon. They also treat apology as a generalisation target, as the thesis says.

findings.part: Whether speech acts are performed in a moment (the synchronic/diachronic premise)
findings.source: "The Apologetic Stance" (author not shown in the snippet), ResearchGate listing
findings.what_they_say: <cite index="25-2">Within speech act theory it is standardly assumed that speech acts are performed in a moment.</cite> The snippet is truncated, but the framing suggests the paper goes on to question that assumption for apology.
findings.note: A referee will ask whether the synchronic/diachronic contrast is stated or contested elsewhere. I could not see the paper's own argument.

findings.part: The presupposition that there is some speaker-unit to be individuated and bound by a promise
findings.what_they_say: <cite index="10-4,10-5">Questions about what 'I' and 'you' refer to, whether systems can lie or be held to promises, and the identity of interlocutors all rest on a false presupposition. There is no speaker behind the screen.</cite>
findings.note: This denies the premise that any unit speaks, for assertion and promising alike. The thesis has to be stated conditionally, on the assumption that artificial speakers are possible at all.

findings.part: The literature groups Freiman & Miller, Green & Michel and Williams & Bayne as one position, and treats the live positions as assertion-only
findings.source: "Speech Acts and Large Language Models" (PhilArchive preprint); "Who asserts when no one asserts?", Synthese, 2026; "Assertion, Accountability, and Large Language Models", Philosophy & Technology, 2026
findings.what_they_say: <cite index="59-4">The Synthese paper treats fictionalism and proto-assertion as contrastive positions and argues that the proxy view is the most promising way to handle responsibility.</cite> <cite index="41-3">The Philosophy & Technology paper lists AI-testimony, proto-assertion and proxy assertion as intermediate positions.</cite> <cite index="40-9">The preprint groups Freiman & Miller, Green & Michel and Williams & Bayne together as holding that LLMs can be speakers.</cite>
findings.note: These recent syntheses frame the dispute around assertion. That is evidence for the thesis's claim about where the field's attention lies, not a rival.

findings.part: Scaffolding can supply a unit that lasts through the satisfaction horizon
findings.source: "Always-On Agents: A Survey of Persistent Memory, State, and Governance in LLM Agents", arXiv 2606.30306, 2026; "Position: Stop Acting Like Language Model Agents Are Normal Agents", arXiv 2502.10420
findings.what_they_say: <cite index="67-4">The survey treats always-on agents as persistent-state systems whose operative system includes commitments, task ledgers, permissions and records.</cite> <cite index="68-11">The position paper says that, without reinserted context, an LLM will not recall commitments from earlier exchanges.</cite>
findings.note: These supply the engineering evidence that persistence is a property of the scaffold and not of the weights. They are not philosophical arguments about promising.

finding.what_is_left: Granting that proto-assertion, quasi-testimony, fictionalism and proxy accounts were built for assertion, and that commissives are already flagged as awkward for memoryless conversational agents, what survives is the more specific claim that the speaker-unit for promising and similar commissives must be fixed by the act's satisfaction horizon. A persisting scaffolded system, or the principal behind it, can serve as that unit, whereas assertion needs no such unit. On this claim, a graded 'quasi-' or 'proto-' status that may be defensible for assertion is not available for promising, so the choice among the four existing positions is relative to act type and not system-wide.
finding.not_found: I found no source that does all of the following together: individuate the speaker-unit separately for each act type by its satisfaction horizon; argue that scaffolding can supply a commissive-capable unit; and argue that proto-assertion is available for assertion but not for promising. Nothing I found covers the 'quasi-promise is incoherent' step. The nearest items are the commissives passage in the 2209.00731 snippet and Magnus et al.'s contrast with Mallory. I read only snippets of both. The search did leave philosophy, but only into computer science and HCI (agent-memory and persona-individuation papers). I did not search psychology, linguistics, economics or sociology on promising, commitment or reputation, for example the developmental psychology of promising, commitment in economics, or user studies of AI promises. That empirical check is therefore incomplete and a clean result there should not be read as absence. I also did not retrieve: the full texts of Freiman & Miller, Williams & Bayne (whether they discuss commissives), Skiba (how he treats promising) and Green & Michel; Butlin & Viebahn, Arora, Löhr, Mallory and Nickel directly; any SEP or handbook entry on promising or on AI speech acts; or the authorship of the 2209.00731 paper, which the snippet did not show. Much of this literature is paywalled.

sep.why: The theses claim that commissives like promising and apology are diachronic acts whose speaker-unit is fixed by satisfaction conditions, unlike synchronic assertion, so they engage speech act theory, the philosophy of promising, and the debate over assertion.

findings.position: Content conditions are one of Searle and Vanderveken's seven components of force. Promising requires a future content under the speaker's control, so the entry already treats commissives and assertion as differing in content conditions.
findings.quote: I can only promise what is in the future and under my control; or, at least, I cannot promise to do anything that it is obvious to myself and my promissee that I cannot do.
findings.note: Gives the thesis a standard hook: the future-conduct condition is a content condition on promising, not on assertion.

findings.position: Commissives are speech acts through which speakers commit themselves to future courses of action. Promising's sincerity condition is an intention, and the promissory commitment persists until retracted or released.
findings.quote: commissives (in which speakers commit themselves to causes or courses of action, e.g. promising and betting)
findings.note: Supports the premise that promising has a temporal commitment structure. The entry says nothing about the speaker persisting through the horizon.

findings.position: Retraction and release: a promise creates a commitment that lasts until the promisee releases the speaker, which presupposes a persisting committed party.
findings.quote: you may allow me on Wednesday to retract the promise I made to you on Monday. In both these cases of assertion and promise, I am now no longer beholden to the commitments that the speech acts engender
findings.note: Shows commitments persist across time. This gives the thesis its 'unit lasting through the horizon' but only implicitly.

findings.position: Assertion also generates lasting commitments (to defend, to retract if challenged) and illocutionary logic carries these commitments forward across speech acts. A referee could say assertion is not requirement-free with respect to persistence.
findings.who: Green; Searle and Vanderveken 1985 on illocutionary commitment
findings.quote: she is obliged to retract P if she is unable to respond to that challenge adequately
findings.note: Threatens 'assertion has no such requirement'. Assertoric commitment to defend or retract also needs a persisting agent, though it is not a content condition.

findings.position: Preparatory conditions and felicity: a speech act can misfire or be an abuse (insincere promise) with respect to the speaker's standing or intention. A system that cannot persist might promise but be insincere, or fail to promise at all.
findings.quote: I promise to meet you for lunch tomorrow, but haven't the least intention of making good. Here I have promised all right, but the act is not felicitous because it is not sincere.
findings.note: Suggests a referee will ask whether lack of a persisting unit means no promise (misfire) or an insincere one (abuse).

findings.position: Whether speech acts require the intention and speaker meaning of the performer. This bears on whether artificial speakers perform speech acts at all, and on speaker meaning without cognitive effect on addressees.
findings.quote: a speech act is a type of act that can be performed by speaker meaning that one is doing so.
findings.note: A referee will say the thesis presupposes that artificial speakers can speaker-mean at all. The entry makes speaker meaning a necessary condition for non-conventional speech acts.

findings.position: Social uptake and standing: a pattern of broken promises or denied uptake can deprive a speaker of the ability to promise at all.
findings.quote: the inveterate promise-breaker will, in time, lead others in his community to be unwilling to accept any promises he tries to make.
findings.note: Relevant to 'scaffolding': the ability to promise depends on community-supplied conditions, not just the speaker's internal resources.

nearest_positions: Searle and Vanderveken's seven components of force, including content conditions and preparatory conditions, under which promising's future-conduct content condition is a feature of the act type

Green's normative-commitment account of force (assertion, conjecture and promise as overt commitments with differing liabilities) together with Sbisà on retraction, which makes commitment persistence central
Austin's felicity conditions (misfire versus abuse), including uptake and the sincerity/intention condition for commissives
per_thesis.entry_silent_on: Artificial or non-human speakers, personal identity or persistence of the speaker across time, and scaffolding or memory architecture as a precondition for commissives. The entry never asks what kind of unit must survive until a promise's satisfaction time. It mentions only a dog requesting to be let out (Searle) and pre-linguistic infants, photocopiers and photographs (Davis 1992), and does not compare speech acts by temporal-persistence demands.

findings.position: Promising treated as a speech act (illocutionary, conventional) in Austin and Searle; the entry frames promising as a form of utterance under conditions, and links it to assertion only via van Roojen and Watson citations. This is the nearest speech-act framing the thesis must be situated against, though nothing about artificial speakers.
findings.who: Austin (1962), Searle (1963, 1965, 1979), Alston, Pratt, Harris & McKinney survey
findings.quote: Austin takes promising to be an illocutionary act, that is, he takes it that promising is merely a matter of a certain form of utterance, under certain conditions.
findings.note: Speech-act framing is available, but the entry offers no account of what the speaker must be to perform it.

findings.position: Promising and assertion are linked in the literature; the entry cites papers on this pairing without describing their content. A referee would raise this against the thesis's promise/assertion contrast.
findings.who: Watson (2004) 'Asserting and Promising'; van Roojen (2020) 'Promising and Assertion'
findings.note: Only the existence of the pairing is reported, not the argument; the entry gives no view on whether assertion and promising differ in persistence requirements.

findings.position: Promissory obligations bind a promisor over time and must be kept later. Hobbes's covenants of trust and Hodgson's point about act utilitarians show that the gap between promise and performance is what generates the problem. This supports a 'satisfaction horizon' that the promisor must last through.
findings.quote: when the time came to keep the promise, the promisor would simply apply the utilitarian calculus, without regard to the fact that he had previously “promised”
findings.note: Gives the thesis a temporal-persistence hook within the promising literature.

findings.position: Self-promises and resolutions are explained as solidifying the will over time, and self-binding as protecting choices from deterioration. This ties promising to a persisting agent across time.
findings.who: Dannenberg (2015); Liberman (2019) on resolutions and vows
findings.quote: self promises are a way of solidifying our wills, protecting our valued choices from deterioration in the face of time and trials
findings.note: Supplies a persistence-of-agent theme the thesis can build on.

findings.position: Problematic promisees (the dead, absent, or unspecified) show that promissory theories test conditions on the promisee's side. The thesis tests the promisor's side, so a referee would ask whether uptake conditions already cover its concern.
findings.quote: promisees who fail to have the standard cognitive capacity to rely on promises would certainly fail the uptake condition
findings.note: Entry's cognitive-capacity worries are about promisees, not promisors.

findings.position: Joint commitment and expectation views impose demanding mental-state requirements. Gilbert requires 'common knowledge' between parties and Scanlon's Principle F requires iterated knowledge and intention. An artificial speaker would have to meet these, which is a nearby route to the thesis's concern.
findings.quote: joint commitment views are similarly cognitively demanding, requiring as they do complex and sophisticated mental states like mutual intentions
findings.note: Sets a competing candidate for what an artificial promisor lacks, other than a persisting unit.

nearest_positions: Conventionalist speech-act view of promising (promising as an illocutionary act performed by a conventional form of utterance) — Austin, Searle
Normative power views grounding promising in the promisor's capacity to bind a future self — Hart, Raz, Owens, Shiffrin
Self-promise/resolution accounts tying promissory obligation to a will that persists over time — Rosati, Dannenberg, Liberman, with Hobbes's release problem
per_thesis.entry_silent_on: Artificial speakers, AI systems, or scaffolding of any kind; the notion of a 'unit capable of lasting through the satisfaction horizon' (a persistence or identity condition on the speaker); any comparison of commissives to assertion in terms of future-conduct content conditions; the possibility of an agent that can assert but not promise. The entry does not discuss personal identity or diachronic agency as a precondition of promising.

findings.position: Promising and asserting generate different kinds of commitment. Promising's primary commitment is to act so that φ happens. Asserting's primary commitment is to facts independent of one's actions, namely the defensibility of p. The entry treats them as different families, which partly backs the thesis's claim that the two acts can come apart. The entry never ties this to artificial speakers or to a persisting agent.
findings.quote: When you promise to φ , your primary commitment is to (intend to) act so as to make φ happen. By contrast, when you assert that p , your primary commitment is to facts that are independent of your actions
findings.note: Supplies the action-directed versus fact-directed asymmetry the thesis needs, but does not say that assertion lacks a persistence requirement.

findings.position: Asserting and promising are closely linked. Marsili says promising that you will φ illocutionarily entails asserting that you will φ, so a promise includes an assertion about future conduct. Hawley analyses assertion as a promise to speak truthfully. If Marsili is right, an assertion with future-conduct content has the same persistence demand as a promise, so assertion is not free of it.
findings.quote: promising that you will do something entails asserting that you will do it.
findings.note: Undermines 'assertion has no such requirement'. Assertions about one's own future conduct, and Hawley's promise to speak truthfully, bring persistence back in.

findings.position: Assertoric commitment is partly a matter of what the speaker is expected to do afterwards: defend the claim if challenged, avoid contradicting it, or retract it. This is a diachronic demand on the asserter. The entry treats it as a commitment that follows from the primary one (Watson), so it is secondary and conditional. That fits the thesis's contrast between a constitutive and a derivative persistence demand.
findings.quote: The speaker's commitment to defend the assertion if challenged is on this view a secondary commitment, that follows from the primary one
findings.note: The accountability and retraction literature imposes a persistence requirement on asserters, which the thesis must address when it says assertion has none.

findings.position: The thesis contrasts commissives with assertion. In Austin's taxonomy, commissives (promising, undertaking) are a separate class from expositives, where assertion is placed. This gives a classificatory basis for treating the acts differently.
findings.quote: a commissive by promising, undertaking or declaring that you will do something
findings.note: Gives a taxonomic footing only. Nothing on artificial speakers.

findings.position: Accounts of assertion that appeal to sanctions, liability and trust (accountability, the Peircean liability account) presuppose a speaker who can be held to account over time. A referee would raise this against the claim that assertion needs no enduring unit.
findings.quote: renders [the speaker] liable to the penalties of the social law (or, at any rate, those of the moral law) in case [the asserted proposition] should not be true
findings.note: Accountability-based accounts need a persisting bearer of liability, which threatens the claim that assertion is unconstrained by persistence.

nearest_positions: Commitment as accountability and as expected future conduct (defend, retract, stay consistent) — Peirce, Alston, Brandom, MacFarlane, Rescorla
Asserting and promising as distinct commitments, with promising future-action-directed and asserting fact-directed — Searle, Watson (2004)
Promising entails or is built on asserting (Marsili 2016) or assertion is built on promising (Hawley 2019)
per_thesis.entry_silent_on: The entry does not discuss artificial speakers, AI systems, scaffolding, or any 'unit capable of lasting through the satisfaction horizon'. It does not treat the persistence or identity conditions of the speaker as a requirement for performing speech acts, and it does not compare acts by their temporal horizon.

theses: For artificial speakers, acts whose content conditions include future conduct by the speaker (promising and similar commissives) depend on whether a unit capable of lasting through the satisfaction horizon is available, and scaffolding can supply one. Assertion has no such requirement, so artificial systems can come apart on the two acts.
